sports.description: Road races on measured, traffic-free courses, from 5 km fun runs to the 42.195 km marathon. Most Indian city races run between October and February and start around sunrise to avoid the heat. timeline.what: Lay out kit, pin the bib, charge the watch, eat a familiar carbohydrate-rich dinner and set two alarms.
Wake up and eat a light, low-fibre carbohydrate breakfast you have tested in training; sip water.
Reach the venue; roads close early for Indian city races and parking or metro queues build fast.
Toilet queue, bag drop, check the course map and aid station positions.
Warm up: 5-10 minutes of easy jogging and strides for 5K/10K; brisk walking and a few strides for half and full.
Enter your start wave or corral; last few sips of water.
Start 10-15 seconds per km slower than goal pace for the first 1-2 km, then settle in.
For races over an hour, take carbohydrate every 30-40 minutes and drink at aid stations to thirst.

timeline.label: Finish to +30 min
timeline.what: Keep walking, drink, eat carbohydrate with some protein, change out of wet clothes and collect your certificate.

nutrition: Under 60 minutes (5K, most 10Ks): water is enough; a normal breakfast 2-3 hours before covers your fuel.
Pre-race meal: 1-4 g of carbohydrate per kg body weight, 1-4 hours before (a 60 kg runner: 60-240 g), low in fat and fibre.
Half marathon (1-2.5 hours): 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour, e.g. one 25 g gel every 30-40 minutes from about 40 minutes in.
Marathon (over 2.5 hours): aim for 60 g per hour; up to 90 g per hour works only with glucose-fructose products practised in training.
Marathon carb-load: 10-12 g of carbohydrate per kg per day for the 36-48 hours before the race.
Fluids: keep body-mass loss under 2%. Weigh yourself before and after a long run: each 1 kg lost is about 1 litre of sweat. Many runners need 400-800 ml per hour.
Do not drink so much that you gain weight during the race; over-drinking can cause dangerously low blood sodium (hyponatraemia).
In humid cities such as Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, use the electrolyte drink at alternate aid stations to replace sweat sodium.
safety: Heat: pre-monsoon (March-June) maxima in north and central India often exceed 40 C. Marathon times slow steadily as heat stress rises, so lower your target on warm mornings.
Stop and get medical help if you feel confused, stumble, stop sweating or vomit: these are signs of exertional heat stroke, an emergency treated by rapid whole-body cooling.
Humidity: in coastal cities sweat does not evaporate well; slow down and follow your drinking plan even if you do not feel hot.

Air quality: check the CPCB AQI the evening before and on race morning. At 201-300 (Poor) cut the warm-up short and avoid all-out efforts; above 300 consider skipping. Delhi NCR is usually Poor or worse from late October to January.
Monsoon (June-September; October-December in Chennai): waterlogged roads hide potholes and open drains; avoid running through floodwater and wear reflective kit under dark skies.
Pre-dawn training: run facing traffic, wear a light or reflective band, and watch for stray dogs.
Get a medical check-up before your first half or full marathon, especially if you are over 35 or have heart disease in the family; never race with a fever.
beginner_tips: Start with run-walk intervals: Couch to 5K takes 9 weeks at 3 sessions a week to reach 30 minutes of running.
Run most of your training at a pace where you can still talk; if you cannot, slow down.
Increase weekly distance gradually and keep 2 rest days a week while you are new.
Nothing new on race day: test your shoes, breakfast and gels on long training runs.
Choose your first race 8-12 weeks away and between October and February for cooler mornings.
Line up in the wave that matches your expected time, not at the front.
Walk through aid stations to drink; it costs seconds and can save minutes later.
If a full marathon is your goal, race a half first: some Indian marathons only accept full entries with a timing certificate.
training: Consistency: 3-4 runs every week matter more than any single big session.
The long run builds endurance: add about 1-1.5 km a week with an easier week every third or fourth week.
Mostly easy: keep most runs conversational (about 65-75% of max heart rate) and add one faster session a week only after 6+ weeks of base.
Progress load gradually; a jump of more than 30% over 2 weeks is linked to more injuries in new runners.
Taper: cut volume in the last 1 week for 5K to half marathon and the last 3 weeks for a marathon, while keeping a little pace work.
Cross-train with cycling, swimming or brisk walking on non-run days to build fitness with less impact.

nutrition: Under 1.5 hours: water and a gel or two is enough.
1-2.5 hours: 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour.
Over 2.5 hours: 60-90 g per hour; amounts near 90 g need glucose-fructose mixes and gut training.
Mix gels with real food in ultras (bananas, chikki, boiled potatoes with salt, idli) because sweet-only fuel gets hard to stomach after 4-5 hours.
Fluids: keep body-mass loss under 2%; start around 400-800 ml per hour and adjust for heat and climbing.
Add sodium (electrolyte drink or salt tabs) on long, hot or humid runs.
Carry enough between aid stations: at least 500 ml per hour of expected running time on the longest gap.
safety: Monsoon (June-September): Western Ghats trails get slippery, streams rise fast and leeches appear; never cross a fast stream above knee depth.
Heat: exposed ridges in March-June can exceed 40 C; run early, carry extra water, and slow down on climbs.
Heat illness: confusion, stumbling or stopping sweating means stop, get shade and call for help; rapid cooling saves lives.
Stay on the marked route; if you have not seen a marker for 500 m, go back to the last one.
Run with the mandatory kit even if it feels heavy; a twisted ankle at night far from an aid station can mean hours of waiting.
Himalayan races above about 2500 m: follow the organiser's acclimatisation days and descend if you get a severe headache, breathlessness at rest or confusion.
Wildlife and dogs: do not approach animals, keep food packed, and follow forest department rules in protected areas.
beginner_tips: Start with a short XXS race and learn to walk the climbs; power-hiking is faster and cheaper than running steep grades.
Train on similar terrain: forts and hill trails near Pune, Mumbai and Bengaluru make good weekend practice.
Shorten your stride and look 2-3 m ahead on descents.
Practise with your vest full so the race weight is not a surprise.
Judge effort by time, not distance: 10 km on trail can take as long as 15 km on road.
Read the race's mandatory kit list early and test everything before race day.
training: Specificity: train on climbs and descents similar to the race; uphill running costs several times more energy than flat running.
Use time-on-feet long runs and back-to-back weekend runs instead of single huge runs.
Build weekly km-effort gradually, about 10% a week, with an easier week every 3-4 weeks.
Strength work twice a week (squats, lunges, step-ups, calf raises) protects knees on long descents.
Practise eating and drinking during every long run.

sports.name: Cycling
sports.description: Road and off-road events: mass-participation cyclothons, chip-timed gran fondos, self-supported brevets (BRMs) and mountain-bike races. In India, BRMs are run only by Audax India Randonneurs under Audax Club Parisien rules; they are not races, and everyone who finishes inside the time limit is a finisher.

disciplines.name: Mountain biking

nutrition: Under 1 hour: water is enough.

safety: Traffic: ride on the left, single file on highways, no earphones; assume trucks and buses have not seen you.

Monsoon: wet roads double braking distance, potholes hide under water, and visibility drops; brake earlier and avoid painted lines.

Group riding: call out potholes, hold your line, and never overlap wheels.

Most riding at easy, conversational effort; one harder session a week (hill repeats or tempo) builds speed.
Ride the terrain you will race: climbs for gran fondos, night rides for 400+ brevets.
Practise eating and drinking on every ride over 90 minutes.
Add 2 short strength sessions a week for core and hips to protect the lower back.

sports.name: Badminton
sports.description: Badminton is played indoors with a feather or nylon shuttle in singles, doubles and mixed doubles. Amateur events in India run from club and corporate tournaments to district, state and BAI ranking events, including Masters age groups from 35+. From 4 January 2027 the BWF default scoring changes to best of three games to 15 points.

disciplines.name: Singles
disciplines.description: One player per side on the narrow singles court; the most running per point.

disciplines.name: Doubles
disciplines.description: Men's or women's pairs on the full-width court; fast drives and attacking rotations.

disciplines.name: Mixed doubles
disciplines.description: One man and one woman per side; usually one player at the net and one at the back.

timeline.what: Check the draw and order of play (BAI draws are often made at the venue a day before). Note your first match number, court and time; pack your kit.
Eat your main pre-match meal and start sipping water.
Arrive at the venue and report to the control desk. Confirm your name in the draw and the reporting rules: missing your call can mean a walkover.
Find your court and listen to the announcement system; check how far behind schedule the matches are running.
Off-court warm-up for 15-20 minutes: easy jog, dynamic mobility, shadow footwork to all four corners, a few explosive lunges.
Small snack or sips of sports drink, re-grip if needed, put on fresh socks, keep warm.
At the court: toss, short knock-up as allowed by the umpire, then play. Use the mid-game and between-game intervals to drink and towel off.
Sign the score sheet if asked, report the result, and check when your next match is.
Refuel and rehydrate based on the gap to your next match; keep moving lightly so you do not stiffen.

nutrition: Plan for each match being 20-40 minutes of near-maximal effort: heart rate averages over 90% of maximum in elite matches, so treat a 3-match day like a long training session.

Eat a carbohydrate-based meal 3-4 hours before your first match (for example poha, 3 idlis with sambar, or rice with dal) and a small snack 60-90 minutes before (a banana or 3-4 dates). Avoid heavy fried food on the day.
Once your total playing time passes about an hour, take 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour of play (USTA guidance). 500 ml of a 6% sports drink gives about 30 g; a medium banana gives about 25 g.

Weigh yourself before and after your first match. Each 1 kg lost is roughly 1 litre of sweat. The ACSM aims to keep losses under 2% of body weight (1.4 kg for a 70 kg player), so drink more in the next match if you lost more.

Replace salt as well as water on hot or humid days: ORS, salted nimbu pani or chaas all help (NCDC). A quarter teaspoon of salt contains about 590 mg of sodium (USTA). Plain water alone after heavy sweating can dilute blood sodium.

Between matches: under 1 hour, sip a sports drink or eat a banana only; 1-2 hours, a light snack such as 2 idlis, a peanut chikki or curd with fruit; over 2 hours, a small meal like curd rice or chapati with dal, finished at least 90 minutes before you play.
After your last match, drink about 1.5 litres for every kg of body weight lost over the next few hours, with a salty meal containing carbohydrate and protein.
Skip alcohol, very sugary soft drinks and large amounts of tea or coffee on hot match days. The NCDC heat advisory notes they can increase fluid loss or cause stomach cramps.
safety: Heatstroke is an emergency: stop play and call 108 if a player becomes confused, staggers, faints, has hot dry skin or a body temperature of 40 C or more. Cool them at once by moving them to shade, pouring cold water over large areas of skin and fanning (NCDC heat advisory).
Painful muscle spasms after long play in heat are heat cramps: rest in a cool place and drink ORS. Get medical help if they last more than an hour (NCDC).

If you have come from a cooler city or are returning after a break, build up exposure to heat gradually over 10-15 days before a hot tournament (NCDC). People with heart disease or high blood pressure are at higher risk and should check with a doctor first.
Many Indian halls are not air-conditioned. In April to June, check the forecast and bring extra fluids; humid halls raise sweat loss even when the temperature looks moderate.
Sweat on the court floor causes slips: ask the umpire to stop play and wipe the wet patch before the next rally.
Lunges and jumps load the ankle, knee and Achilles tendon. Warm up properly and stop if you feel a sudden pop or sharp pain at the back of the heel.
In doubles, keep your racket up at the net and agree with your partner who takes shots down the middle to avoid racket clashes.
If you are over 35 and new to competitive play, or have heart or blood pressure problems, get a medical check-up before a multi-match day.
beginner_tips: Scoring basics: every rally wins a point. Until 3 January 2027 most events play best of 3 games to 21 (at 20-all you need a 2-point lead, capped at 30). From 4 January 2027 the BWF default is games to 15, with the 21st point winning at 20-all. Check the prospectus.

The server serves from the right court when their score is even and from the left when it is odd. The shuttle must be hit below the server's waist line set in the Laws; ask the umpire which service rule the event uses.
Report on time and stay within earshot of announcements. If you are not at the court when called, the referee can award a walkover.
Test the shuttle with the umpire before the match and agree on a shuttle change if it gets damaged; do not change shuttles repeatedly to delay play.
When there are no line judges, call lines on your side honestly and give the benefit of the doubt to your opponent.
Shake hands with your opponent and the umpire after the match, win or lose.
In your first tournament, enter one event. You will learn the routine without being overloaded.
training: Train in the work-rest pattern of matches: badminton rallies last about 7 seconds with about 15 seconds of rest, so use interval drills like 8 seconds of shadow footwork, 15 seconds of rest, repeated in sets.
Footwork first: most points are lost by being late to the shuttle. Two short footwork sessions a week improve every shot.
Increase training load in small steps, for example 10-15 minutes more court time per week, and keep at least one full rest day.
Play matches against slightly better players at least once a week; match play builds decision-making that drills do not.
Strengthen legs and core twice a week (squats, lunges, calf raises, planks) to protect knees and ankles.
Reduce training volume in the last week before the event so you start the day fresh.

sports.name: Tennis
sports.description: Tennis is played outdoors in India on hard and clay courts, in singles and doubles. Amateur options include club ladders, corporate and NTRP-style level events, veterans age groups and AITA ranking tournaments for juniors (U-12 to U-18) and adults. Matches usually last 60-90 minutes, so heat and back-to-back matches are the main event-day challenges.

beginner_tips: Scoring basics: points go 15, 30, 40, game; at 40-40 (deuce) you need two points in a row, unless the event uses no-ad scoring, where the next point wins. A set is first to 6 games by 2, with a tie-break at 6-6.
Many amateur events replace the third set with a 10-point match tie-break (first to 10, win by 2). Check before you start.
Without an umpire, you call the lines on your side. Call the ball out only if you clearly see space between the ball and the line; any doubt goes to your opponent.
Announce the score before each first serve so there is no argument later.
If a ball rolls onto your court during a point, call 'let' at once and replay the point.
Do not walk behind a court while a point is being played; wait for the end of the point.
Bring your own balls for warm-up and arrive early: late sign-in can mean losing by default.
training: Most amateur matches are decided by serve and return; spend a quarter of practice time on them.
Train for 60-90 minutes of play with bursts: interval runs of 10-20 seconds hard, 20-30 seconds easy match the stop-start nature of points.
Play at the time of day your event is scheduled so your body gets used to the heat.
Increase match play gradually and keep at least one full rest day a week to protect the shoulder and elbow.
Add two short strength sessions a week (legs, core, shoulder external rotation) to reduce injury risk.

nutrition: Plan for repeated sprints across several short matches: total playing time in a 5-a-side day can pass 90 minutes, which is a full-match workload in heat on turf.

Eat a carbohydrate-based meal 3-4 hours before your first match (for example poha, 3 idlis with sambar, or rice with dal) and a small snack 60-90 minutes before (a banana or 3-4 dates). Avoid heavy fried food on the day.
Once your total playing time passes about an hour, take 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour of play (USTA guidance). 500 ml of a 6% sports drink gives about 30 g; a medium banana gives about 25 g.

Weigh yourself before and after your first match. Each 1 kg lost is roughly 1 litre of sweat. The ACSM aims to keep losses under 2% of body weight (1.4 kg for a 70 kg player), so drink more in the next match if you lost more.

Replace salt as well as water on hot or humid days: ORS, salted nimbu pani or chaas all help (NCDC). A quarter teaspoon of salt contains about 590 mg of sodium (USTA). Plain water alone after heavy sweating can dilute blood sodium.

Between matches: under 1 hour, sip a sports drink or eat a banana only; 1-2 hours, a light snack such as 2 idlis, a peanut chikki or curd with fruit; over 2 hours, a small meal like curd rice or chapati with dal, finished at least 90 minutes before you play.
After your last match, drink about 1.5 litres for every kg of body weight lost over the next few hours, with a salty meal containing carbohydrate and protein.
Skip alcohol, very sugary soft drinks and large amounts of tea or coffee on hot match days. The NCDC heat advisory notes they can increase fluid loss or cause stomach cramps.
safety: Heatstroke is an emergency: stop play and call 108 if a player becomes confused, staggers, faints, has hot dry skin or a body temperature of 40 C or more. Cool them at once by moving them to shade, pouring cold water over large areas of skin and fanning (NCDC heat advisory).
Painful muscle spasms after long play in heat are heat cramps: rest in a cool place and drink ORS. Get medical help if they last more than an hour (NCDC).

If you have come from a cooler city or are returning after a break, build up exposure to heat gradually over 10-15 days before a hot tournament (NCDC). People with heart disease or high blood pressure are at higher risk and should check with a doctor first.

For outdoor football in India, avoid playing in direct sun between 12:00 and 15:00 where you can (NCDC advisory) and ask the organiser about morning or evening slots. Humidity above about 70% on the coast (Mumbai, Chennai, Kochi) slows sweat evaporation, so you heat up faster at the same temperature.
Use WBGT where the organiser has a meter: FIFPRO recommends cooling breaks from about 26-28 C WBGT and moving matches above 32 C; FIFA makes cooling breaks mandatory above 32 C.
Remove all jewellery before playing; the Laws ban it and taping over it is not allowed.
Clean turf burns with water and antiseptic straight away; they get infected easily in heat.
Ankle sprains and hamstring strains are the most common injuries in small-sided games: warm up fully and do not play on through a sprain.
beginner_tips: Read the event rules before you arrive: 5-a-side often has a head-height rule (no passes or shots above head height) and a goalkeeper area that outfield players cannot enter.
Rolling substitutions are usually allowed in 5s and 7s: the player coming off must leave the pitch before the substitute enters.
Scoring and standings: group stages usually give 3 points for a win and 1 for a draw, then goal difference. Check how ties in knockouts are decided (often penalties).
Only the captain should speak to the referee; arguing over calls wastes time and can earn cards.
Be at your pitch before the scheduled time: many organisers award the match to the other team if you are not ready.
Shake hands with the other team and the referee after each match.
training: Train for repeated sprints, not just long runs: small-sided football is short bursts with brief recoveries.
Play small-sided games in training with your actual team to build understanding and passing patterns.
Build training load gradually, and include hamstring and groin strength work (for example Nordic curls and Copenhagen planks) twice a week.
Do your harder sessions at the time of day your tournament matches are scheduled to adapt to the heat.
Cut back training in the last few days before the tournament so legs are fresh.
